newsitem.title: JORDAN: Turkey, Jordan discuss economic and defence ties.
newsitem.headline: Turkey, Jordan discuss economic and defence ties.

text.p: Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller held talks on Monday with Jordan's King Hussein and Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti on economic and defence cooperation.
"We are looking into projects in water and electricity, sharing in defence cooperation if possible," Ciller told Kabariti at the start of their talks.
"And also definitely we will be in position to give support to you in the endeavours you have initiated in the peace process in the Middle East," she added.
Ciller, accompanied by several ministers and a group of businessmen, later told a business gathering her country could be a bridge linking Jordanian exporters to markets in Europe and Central Asia.
The two countries, both neighbours of Iraq, discussed the damage to their economies caused by trade sanctions imposed on Baghdad six years ago because of its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

"We discussed the role Turkey could play in pushing the peace process forward, the situation in Iraq, and to what extent Jordan and Turkey could coordinate their stands to lift the blockade on the Iraqi people," Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti was quoted as saying by the Petra news agency.
Ciller's trip was scheduled for September but was delayed by the crisis following Baghdad's intervention in northern Iraq in support of a rebel Kurdish faction.

Ciller arrived two days after Jordanian and Turkish air commanders held talks in Amman. The two countries have allowed U.S. planes to patrol no-fly zones over northern and southern Iraq respectively from their own territory.

Jordan was one of the few Arab countries not to criticise a proposed Turkish security zone in north Iraq against Turkish Kurd rebels forces. The buffer plan was announced in September but has not yet been put in force.

Jordan, the Arab state with warmest ties to Israel, also defended a defence training pact signed by Turkey and the Jewish state earlier this year. Syria, bordered by Jordan, Turkey and Israel, had strongly criticised it is an attempt at encirclement.
Kabariti told Ciller, whose True Path Party formed a coalition government with the Islamist Welfare Party, that their two countries were models of religious tolerance in the region.

"We ought to feel that Turkey and Jordan could really be trendsetters and could portray themselves as the champions of the policy of inclusion," said Kabariti, whose government faces fierce opposition from Jordan's largest parliamentary party, the Islamic Action Front.
"We have given Islam and Moslems the right portrait -- the portrait of democracy, of moderation," Kabariti said.
